456.title: Chukat: the red heifer (Numbers 19)
456.hook: a ritual that purifies the impure and defiles the pure; tradition says even Solomon couldn't explain it
456.howItsDone: Besides the weekly reading of Chukat, the red heifer chapter is read again on Shabbat Parah, a special Sabbath before Passover, recalling the purification once needed before the festival.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aaron's staff put out buds, blossoms and ripe almonds overnight, and the Korach story ended with something growing. Your line was the staff blossoms. What did you see coming back to life? Day four hundred fifty-six.

Why is the sky blue? Why do we have to? Why? Why? A small child can keep that up until the grown-up in the room runs out and says, because. Grown-ups tend to hope that with enough study, everything eventually has a because. Then comes this week's Torah portion, Chukat, and the ritual it opens with is one that Jewish tradition itself says nobody has fully explained. A rare red cow, burned to ash. The ash makes people pure. And the people who prepare it become impure. Today, a law with no because.
screen: `WHY? WHY? WHY?` → `A RARE RED COW, BURNED TO ASH.` → `A LAW WITH NO BECAUSE.`

segments.voice: The ritual, in paraphrase, goes like this. Find a red heifer, a young cow, completely red, with no blemish, that has never worn a yoke. She is slaughtered outside the camp and burned, with cedar wood, hyssop and scarlet thread thrown into the fire. Her ashes are kept and mixed with fresh water. Anyone who has touched a dead body is sprinkled with that water on the third day and the seventh day, and becomes pure again. Then the twist: the priest who prepares it, and the one who burns it, become impure themselves, until evening. The same ashes that cleanse one person make another unclean. The chapter opens with the words chukat ha-Torah, the statute of the Torah. A chok, in the rabbis' vocabulary, is a law given without a stated reason, alongside mishpatim, laws anyone could work out for themselves, like don't steal. A midrash says King Solomon, famous for his wisdom, understood every law but this one, and quoted his own words from Ecclesiastes: I said, I will be wise, but it was far from me. Another midrash tells of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai. A non-Jew asks him about the ritual, and he gives a clever answer. Afterward his students say, you pushed him off; what do you tell us? And he says, in paraphrase: the dead don't make impure, and the water doesn't make pure. It is a decree, and we keep it. Jewish thinkers have held different views since. Maimonides held that every commandment has a purpose, even when we can't see it. Others treat the chok as a lesson in trust. Both keep the law.
screen: `ASHES THAT CLEANSE, AND DEFILE.` · `CHOK: A LAW WITH NO STATED REASON.` · `EVEN SOLOMON: IT WAS FAR FROM ME.` · `IT IS A DECREE, AND WE KEEP IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept one thing you don't understand. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something in your life you've never been able to explain. A loss. A person you love who does something you can't fathom. A question about God, or about yourself. Don't try to solve it now. Just hold it, the way you'd hold a stone in your hand, and say to yourself, I don't understand this, and it's still here. Notice whether the not-knowing can sit beside you without a fight. Breathe until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Chok. A statute, a law given without a stated reason. The red heifer is the classic chok: ashes that make one person pure and another impure.
Your line: not everything explains itself. Today, when something doesn't make sense, try saying I don't know yet, instead of inventing a reason. Day four hundred fifty-six.

457.title: Chukat: Miriam's well (Numbers 20:1–2)
457.hook: Miriam dies and the water stops; the Talmud says a well went with them for her sake (Taanit 9a)
457.howItsDone: Miriam's death is read in synagogue as part of the portion of Chukat; today some families place a cup of water for Miriam, called Miriam's cup, on the Passover seder table.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the red heifer: ashes that cleanse one person and make another impure, a chok with no stated reason. Your line was not everything explains itself. Did you let one thing stay unexplained? Day four hundred fifty-seven.

Some people hold a family together so quietly that nobody notices until they're gone. The grandmother whose kitchen was where everyone ended up. The coworker who refilled the coffee and remembered birthdays. After the funeral, something stops working, and only then does everyone realize who was doing it. The Torah has a verse like that. In one short line, Miriam, the sister of Moses and Aaron, dies and is buried. And in the very next line, there's no water.
screen: `THE ONE WHO HELD IT TOGETHER.` → `MIRIAM DIES.` → `THEN THERE'S NO WATER.`

segments.voice: The Torah's words are spare. In paraphrase: the people came to the wilderness of Zin and stayed at Kadesh, and Miriam died there and was buried there. Then: there was no water for the congregation. That's all. No weeping is recorded for her, no days of mourning, nothing like what the Torah will record for Aaron and later for Moses. But the rabbis read the two verses together and heard something. In the Talmud, tractate Taanit, Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehuda teaches that three good leaders rose up for Israel: Moses, Aaron and Miriam. And three good gifts came through them: the manna, for Moses' sake; the clouds of glory, for Aaron's sake; and the well, for Miriam's sake. A well of water traveled with the people through the desert, the rabbis say, because of her. When she died, the well went dry, and that's why the very next verse says there was no water. Why Miriam and water? Look at her story. As a girl, tradition says, she was the sister who stood by the Nile, watching her baby brother float in a basket among the reeds. At the Sea, she took a timbrel and led the women in song after they crossed the water. Water follows her all the way through. The Torah never mentions a well; this is the rabbis reading between two verses. But the picture has stayed. Today some families set a cup of water for Miriam on their Passover table. The well was her quiet gift. Nobody named it while it flowed.
screen: `SHE DIED; THERE WAS NO WATER.` · `THREE LEADERS, THREE GIFTS.` · `THE WELL, FOR MIRIAM'S SAKE.` · `WATER ALL THROUGH HER STORY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank someone who quietly sustained you. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself: who has been a well in my life? Someone who kept things flowing without asking for credit. A parent, a teacher, a neighbor, a friend who always checked in. Picture them clearly. If they're living, decide how you'll thank them this week, in a message, a call, a note. If they've died, simply hold their name for a few breaths, and say it quietly if you'd like. Breathe until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Chukat. The portion where Miriam dies, the water stops, and the rabbis hear a well that had followed her all along.
Your line: miriam's well. Today, notice one thing that works only because someone quietly keeps it working, and tell them you noticed. Day four hundred fifty-seven.

what it means: the rabbis' reading that water followed the people through the desert because of Miriam, and stopped when she died.
what a scholar hears: Taanit 9a builds it from the juxtaposition of Numbers 20:1 and 20:2, giving each of the three siblings a gift: manna, clouds, well.

458.title: Chukat: striking the rock (Numbers 20:7–12)
458.hook: told to speak to the rock, Moses strikes it, and will not enter the land
458.howItsDone: The waters of Meribah are read in the portion of Chukat, and Jewish commentaries, from Rashi and Maimonides to modern teachers, are studied side by side because they disagree about what Moses did wrong.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Miriam died, the water stopped, and the rabbis heard a well that had followed her all along. Your line was miriam's well. Who did you thank for keeping things flowing? Day four hundred fifty-eight.

The water is gone, and the complaining starts almost at once. Why did you bring us out of Egypt, the people say, to this terrible place, with no figs, no vines, no pomegranates, and no water to drink? Moses has heard this speech before. Long before, at a place called Horeb, the people were thirsty, and God told him to strike a rock with his staff, and water poured out. Now he's older. His sister has just died. And this time, the instruction is different by one word.
screen: `NO FIGS, NO VINES, NO WATER.` → `AT HOREB: STRIKE THE ROCK.` → `THIS TIME, ONE WORD DIFFERENT.`

segments.voice: God tells Moses to take the staff, gather the people, and, in the words of the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "speak ye unto the rock before their eyes," so it will give its water. Speak. Not strike. Moses and Aaron gather the people before the rock, and Moses says, "Hear now, ye rebels." Then he lifts his hand and strikes the rock with his staff, twice. Water gushes out, plenty for everyone and their animals. And then the verdict, in paraphrase: because you did not trust Me, to make Me holy in the eyes of the people, you will not bring this community into the land. Readers struggle with that sentence. What exactly was the sin? The commentators argue about it, and they don't agree. Rashi says it's in the plain story: he was told to speak, and he struck. Maimonides says it was the anger in hear now, ye rebels, because a leader's anger teaches the people that God is angry. Others point to the words that came next, which in paraphrase ask: shall we bring water out of this rock? As if the miracle were theirs. Some teachers today add a quieter reading. At Horeb, striking was right. But a new generation needed a new way of being led, and the old move, the one that had worked before, was no longer the right one. Whatever the reading, the Torah holds even Moses to the difference between speaking and striking.
screen: `SPEAK YE UNTO THE ROCK.` · `HEAR NOW, YE REBELS, AND HE STRIKES.` · `RASHI, MAIMONIDES: WHAT WAS THE SIN?` · `A NEW GENERATION, A NEW WAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak instead of striking. Settle, and breathe. Think of one situation where you usually reach for the staff: raising your voice, a sharp word, a slammed door, a cold silence. Something that worked once, maybe, and has become a habit. Picture that moment coming tomorrow. Now picture yourself speaking instead, slowly, in a lower voice. What would you actually say? Find the first sentence, and keep it. Breathe with it until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Chukat. The portion where Moses, told to speak to the rock, strikes it instead, and learns he won't enter the land.
Your line: speak to the rock. Today, the next time you feel the urge to snap, lower your voice instead and say one plain sentence. Day four hundred fifty-eight.

459.title: Chukat: Aaron dies (Numbers 20:22–29)
459.hook: all the house of Israel weeps thirty days for the man who pursued peace
459.howItsDone: Aaron's death is read in the portion of Chukat, and Hillel's saying about being a student of Aaron, loving and pursuing peace, is among the best-known lines of Pirkei Avot, often taught to children.

segments.voice: Yesterday, told to speak to the rock, Moses struck it, and the commentators still argue about why that mattered so much. Your line was speak to the rock. Did you lower your voice once? Day four hundred fifty-nine.

At some funerals the room is full of people who don't seem to fit together. Old rivals standing side by side. A cousin who hasn't spoken to the family in years. Neighbors nobody recognizes. And when you ask, the answer is usually the same: he was the one who made peace. He'd call both sides. He smoothed things over. The Torah describes a mourning like that. Not long after Miriam's death, the people reach a mountain called Hor, and Aaron, the first high priest, climbs it for the last time.
screen: `OLD RIVALS SIDE BY SIDE.` → `THE ONE WHO MADE PEACE.` → `AARON CLIMBS MOUNT HOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the scene, in paraphrase. God tells Moses to take Aaron and his son Eleazar up Mount Hor, in sight of the whole community. On the mountain, Moses takes off Aaron's priestly garments, the ones we watched being made in Exodus, and puts them on Eleazar. Aaron dies there, on the top of the mountain. Moses and Eleazar come down. There's no speech, no last words. Then the people see that Aaron is gone, and the Torah says they wept for Aaron thirty days, "even all the house of Israel." All the house. The rabbis noticed that phrase. Rashi says it means everyone, men and women alike, because Aaron pursued peace, making peace between people who had quarreled and between husbands and wives. A collection called Avot de-Rabbi Natan tells how he did it. When two people had fallen out, Aaron would go to the first and sit with him and say, your friend is beating his chest, saying, how can I face him, I wronged him. Then he'd go to the second and say the same thing. When the two met, they embraced. It's a gentle story, and a slightly mischievous one: Aaron helped each person believe the other wanted to make up, until they did. Hillel, in the Mishnah, made Aaron the model for everyone: be among the students of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace. Pursuing. Peace in this picture isn't something you wait for. You run after it. And when the man who ran after it died, the tradition says, everyone came.
screen: `THE GARMENTS PASS TO ELEAZAR.` · `ALL THE HOUSE OF ISRAEL WEPT.` · `HE WENT TO EACH SIDE.` · `LOVING PEACE, PURSUING PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember a peacemaker. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you've known who brought people back together: the one who made the first phone call, who sat with both sides, who wouldn't let a family drift apart. They might be living, or they might be gone. Picture their face and the way they did it. If it's someone you've lost, let yourself miss them for a few breaths. If they're still here, consider telling them what they did. Breathe until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Chukat. The portion where Aaron dies on Mount Hor, and all the house of Israel weeps thirty days for the man who pursued peace.
Your line: all the house wept. Today, if you know two people who've drifted apart, say one kind true thing about each to the other. Day four hundred fifty-nine.

460.title: Chukat: look up (Numbers 21:4–9)
460.hook: looking at the copper serpent heals; the Mishnah says it was turning hearts toward heaven (Rosh Hashanah 3:8)
460.howItsDone: The copper serpent is read in the portion of Chukat, and the Mishnah's teaching about it, that healing came when Israel looked upward and turned their hearts to heaven, is often studied alongside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aaron died on Mount Hor, and all the house of Israel wept thirty days for the man who pursued peace. Your line was all the house wept. Who's the peacemaker you remembered? Day four hundred sixty.

How much of your day is spent looking down? At a phone, a keyboard, a sink full of dishes, the next step on the sidewalk. Your neck probably knows the answer better than you do. The Torah has a story where looking up is the cure, quite literally. The people are walking the long way around the land of Edom. They're tired, they're sick of the manna, and they complain again. And then the snakes come.
screen: `HOW MUCH OF YOUR DAY IS LOOKING DOWN?` → `THE LONG WAY AROUND EDOM.` → `THEN THE SNAKES COME.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase, it goes like this. Fiery serpents bite the people, and many die. The people come to Moses and say, we've sinned; pray that the snakes go away. Moses prays. And God's answer is not to remove the snakes. Instead: make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole, and in the words of the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "every one that is bitten, when he seeth it, shall live." Moses makes a serpent of copper and raises it high, and whoever is bitten looks at it and lives. In Hebrew there's a little echo: a nachash, a serpent, made of nechoshet, copper. The rabbis were uneasy about this. A metal snake that heals? In the Mishnah, tractate Rosh Hashanah, they ask, in paraphrase: does a serpent kill, or a serpent bring life? No. When Israel looked upward and turned their hearts to their Father in heaven, they were healed; and if not, they wasted away. So the object isn't the point. The looking up is. The Mishnah says the same about Moses' raised hands in the battle with Amalek: the hands didn't win the war; the people looking up did. And the serpent has a second life. It was kept, and the book of Kings says that in the days of King Hezekiah people were burning incense to it, and calling it Nehushtan. Hezekiah smashed it to pieces. The sign that once pointed upward had become something people stared at instead. Look up, the Mishnah says, not at the pole.
screen: `A SERPENT ON A POLE.` · `NACHASH, NECHOSHET: SERPENT, COPPER.` · `WHEN THEY LOOKED UPWARD, THEY HEALED.` · `HEZEKIAH SMASHES NEHUSHTAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look up for one minute. If you can, step outside or go to a window. If not, simply raise your eyes to the highest point in the room. Let your chin lift a little and your shoulders drop. Look at the sky, or the ceiling, or the top of a tree. Notice how far up it goes. Breathe slowly. If you pray, this is a natural moment to turn your heart upward, the way the Mishnah describes. If you don't, just let your gaze rest somewhere higher than your worries. Stay there until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Chukat. The portion where a copper serpent on a pole heals those who look up, and the Mishnah says it was the looking up that healed.
Your line: look up and live. Today, three times, when you catch yourself looking down at a screen, lift your eyes for one full breath. Day four hundred sixty.

461.title: Balak: a hired curse (Numbers 22:2–6)
461.hook: the king of Moab pays the prophet Balaam to curse Israel
461.howItsDone: The portion of Balak is read in synagogue in the yearly cycle; its story is told almost entirely from outside the camp of Israel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a copper serpent on a pole, and the Mishnah's teaching that it was the looking up that healed. Your line was look up and live. Did you lift your eyes from the screen? Day four hundred sixty-one.

A glowing review of a hotel, written by someone the hotel paid. A study about sugar, funded by a sugar company. An expert on the news who turns out to work for the people he's defending. Behind each one sits a plain question worth asking before believing anything: who's paying for this? The Torah has a story built around that question. A new portion begins today, and for once the Israelites barely appear in it. The whole story happens on the other side of the hill, where a frightened king is reaching for his wallet.
screen: `A PAID REVIEW, A FUNDED STUDY.` → `WHO'S PAYING FOR THIS?` → `A FRIGHTENED KING, ACROSS THE HILL.`

segments.voice: Balak, son of Zippor, is king of Moab. He has seen what Israel did to the Amorites, and Moab is terrified. In the text's vivid picture, paraphrased, this crowd will lick up everything around us the way an ox licks up the grass of the field. So Balak doesn't raise an army. He hires a curse. He sends messengers to a seer named Balaam, son of Beor, who lives far off by the River, with a request: come and curse this people for me. And then the flattery that sounds like a sales pitch. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "for I know that he whom thou blessest is blessed, and he whom thou cursest is cursed." The elders set out with the fees for divination in their hands. Payment up front. Two surprises here. First, Balaam may not be only a character in a story. Archaeologists working at a site called Deir Alla, in Jordan, found an ancient plaster inscription that speaks of Balaam son of Beor, a seer of the gods. So a seer by that name was remembered outside the Bible too. Second, the rabbis read Balaam as someone whose gift was for sale. In Pirkei Avot, they contrast the students of Abraham, who have a generous eye, a humble spirit and a modest appetite, with the students of Balaam, who have a grudging eye, a proud spirit and a greedy appetite. And notice the portion's name, taken from its opening words. It isn't Balaam, after the prophet. It's Balak, the man with the money.
screen: `BALAK: A KING AFRAID.` · `HE WHOM THOU CURSEST IS CURSED.` · `DEIR ALLA: BALAAM IN PLASTER.` · `NAMED FOR THE MAN WITH THE MONEY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice who's paying for an opinion. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one opinion you picked up recently: about a product, a person, a piece of news, maybe even about yourself. Trace it back. Where did it come from? Did someone gain anything by your believing it? There's no need to be cynical; many opinions are honest. Just look for the hand on the wallet, if there is one. Then let the question go, and simply breathe until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Balak. The king of Moab who tried to buy a curse, and the name of the portion that tells the story of the prophet he hired.
Your line: who's paying. Today, when an ad, a post or a pitch tries to change your mind, ask that question once before you agree. Day four hundred sixty-one.

screen: `DAY 461 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BALAK: THE DONKEY SAW FIRST.`

462.title: Balak: the donkey saw first (Numbers 22:21–35)
462.hook: the donkey sees the angel before the famous prophet does
462.tomorrow: Balak: only the word I'm given
462.howItsDone: Balaam's talking donkey is read in synagogue in the portion of Balak, and it is often retold for children, with the donkey's question at the center.

segments.voice: Yesterday, King Balak of Moab sent fees for divination to hire the seer Balaam to curse Israel. Your line was who's paying. Did you catch a hand on a wallet? Day four hundred sixty-two.

The dog won't go down the stairs. The toddler points at something in the corner of the room. The quiet intern says, I think the numbers are wrong. It's easy to brush them off; the experts are in charge. Balaam is the expert in this story, a seer a king will pay to see what others can't. He sets off on the road to Moab, riding his own donkey, the one he's ridden all his life. And on that road, the donkey sees something he doesn't.
screen: `THE DOG WON'T GO DOWN THE STAIRS.` → `THE HIRED SEER ON THE ROAD.` → `THE DONKEY SEES SOMETHING.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase: an angel of God stands in the road with a drawn sword. The donkey sees it and swerves into a field. Balaam beats her back onto the road. Then the path narrows between two vineyard walls. The angel stands there, and the donkey presses against the wall and crushes Balaam's foot. He beats her again. Then a place so narrow there's no way to turn at all. The donkey lies down under him, and Balaam, furious, beats her with his staff. Three times she saw. Three times he struck. Then God opens the donkey's mouth, and she asks, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "What have I done unto thee, that thou hast smitten me these three times?" Balaam answers her, as if talking donkeys were normal: you've made a fool of me; if I had a sword in my hand, I'd kill you. The rabbis enjoyed the irony. Here's a man setting out to destroy a whole nation with his words, and he can't handle his donkey without a sword. Then the donkey asks, gently, haven't I carried you all your life? Have I ever done this before? And he has to say: no. Only then does God open Balaam's eyes, and he sees the angel. The Mishnah, in Pirkei Avot, lists the mouth of the donkey among ten things God created at twilight on the eve of the very first Sabbath, as if it had been waiting since creation for this one conversation. The hired seer saw last. The humble animal saw first, and the best thing it did was ask a question.
screen: `AN ANGEL WITH A DRAWN SWORD.` · `THREE TIMES SHE SAW, THREE TIMES HE STRUCK.` · `HAVE I EVER DONE THIS BEFORE?` · `TEN THINGS MADE AT TWILIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to a humble voice. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone whose warnings you tend to wave away. A child, an older parent, a junior colleague, a friend who's usually quiet. Has that voice been trying to tell you something? Imagine them asking you the donkey's question: have I ever steered you wrong before? Let the answer come honestly. Then take one more slow breath and let it rest until the bell. The bell holds the time.

Balak. The portion where a donkey sees the angel before the prophet does. And this week: the red heifer, Miriam's well, the rock, Aaron's death, the copper serpent, a hired curse, and now a donkey who saw first.
Your line: the donkey saw first. Today, when someone you usually overlook raises a concern, stop and ask them what they're seeing. Day four hundred sixty-two.
